Your step-by-step course for building a property rental business for passive income, {1}even without owning property.{2}
We’re so happy you’re here. This course is everything we’ve learned in almost 10 years of hosting, turned into clear steps you can follow at your own pace.

Imagine having beautiful homes around the world. Places you can stay, rent out, and return to anytime. If you’ve ever dreamed of creating a business that gives you freedom, flexibility and income without being tied to a desk or needing to own real estate, this course is for YOU.

We created this course to help you{1} launch, run and scale a profitable hosting business that works for you, not the other way around.{2} Inside, you’ll find a step-by-step roadmap built from real experience. It teaches you how we did it and how you can too.

{1}In Part 1, we lay the foundation.{2} You’ll learn about the different business models (including how to start without buying property), how to get legally set up, build the right mindset and find your first profitable property even if pitching landlords makes you nervous.

{1}In Part 2, we focus on launching your listing and welcoming your first guests.{2} You’ll learn how to set up and furnish your listing, write a profile that sells, and manage your space efficiently with streamlined systems.

{1}In Part 3, we scale it up to 6 figures.{2} Learn how to automate tasks, build your dream team and expand without burning out. This is where your listing becomes a true business that generates passive income.
We’ve included everything you need: ready-to-use templates, calculators, scripts, real case studies and tools that remove the guesswork and save you hours.
Let’s build something profitable, sustainable, and designed for the lifestyle you actually want.

This course is designed to walk you step by step through launching and growing your hosting business. You’ll find{1} clear instructions, practical tasks, and real-world strategies{2} that have been tested and refined over years of experience.

At certain points, you’ll be given {1}specific action tasks to complete.{2} You can find all of them organized inside {3}your launch roadmap{4}, here in the course. Use it to stay on track, mark your progress, and avoid feeling overwhelmed.
You’ll also see {1}ready-to-use AI prompts {2}throughout the course. They help you write faster and get better results with less effort.
Use this course as your playbook. Take it one step at a time, stay consistent, and don’t let small setbacks slow you down.

Do you have what it takes?
Running a hosting business can be fun, rewarding and highly profitable, but it also takes the right mindset.

The truth is, {1}things will occasionally get damaged.{2} Sometimes you have to deal with bad guests, but it’s part of the game. That’s why you have a team that helps you, and why Airbnb offers host protection.

99% of the guests are amazing, respectful, kind, and grateful, but there is always that 1% who cause problems, complain unfairly, or try to get a discount by pointing out minor flaws. But honestly, it’s all worth it.
“99% of the guests you’ll receive are awesome, but oh, that 1%…”

Also remember,{1} people are out of their usual routine.{2} They might be jet-lagged, hungry, tired, or stressed and sometimes they will react in a totally unreasonable way. Your job (or your manager’s) is not to take things personally, and to stay calm and professional.

You’ll learn so much along the way: not just about hosting, but about people. It’s fascinating to see how different guests are, how cultures interact, and how you grow by learning to stay calm in unexpected situations.
This journey will challenge you, shape you, and help you grow both as a business owner and as a person.
Besides the profit, the experience alone is worth it. {1}Building a business is one of the best forms of self-development you can ever give yourself.{2}

In the beginning, things like a bad review or a difficult guest might affect you a lot. But with every situation you handle, you become stronger and more resilient, and after a while you’ll deal with them much more easily.

From being broke and sleeping on the couch to a 6-figure business that runs by itself and multiple homes around the world.
We both left our hometown with our entire life in a suitcase

In our early twenties, we both left our home countries behind (Belgium and Brazil) and moved to Barcelona with nothing but a suitcase, a little savings, and a whole lot of uncertainty. No safety net. No family nearby. Just the belief that{1} there had to be more to life than doing things the “normal” way.{2}
In 2017, Farah rented a room from Daniel

Daniel was living in a tiny room while he was renting out the bigger rooms of his shared rental apartment. It was actually a {1}walk-in closet with no exterior windows{2}, turned into a bedroom. Farah rented one of those bigger rooms, and that’s how {3}we met: as housemates in a shared apartment{4},{5} both trying to make ends meet in one of Europe’s most expensive cities.{6}
Farah got her own rental apartment (and ended up broke)

After a few months, Farah moved into her own place. After paying a huge deposit and buying the basics, {1}she had only €67.50 left in her bank account.{2} She even found some of her furniture on the street and made a bed from pallets. Rent was high, savings were gone, and things were getting tight. Going back to cold Belgium because the money ran out? She wasn’t going to let that happen. So she got creative.

Farah sublet her bedroom and sometimes slept on the couch, behind a giant beach blanket she hung from a hook above the fridge to the curtain railing by the window. {1}It wasn’t glamorous, but it worked.{2}
The “wait a second…” moment: let’s go all in
At first, it was just a way to help pay the rent. But soon we realized… {1}WAIT. We can actually make serious money doing this?!{2}
We couldn’t afford a team yet, so we both did everything ourselves: cleaning, check-ins, guest messages and maintenance, even watching YouTube tutorials on how to fix a toilet.
We built systems and started working smarter, not harder

We set up self-check-in and automated messages, and hired our first cleaner. {1}Every euro we made, we reinvested, and we made sacrifices.{2} We also upgraded the furniture and made every room more beautiful for a better guest experience. {3}Little by little, the business started running without needing us 24/7.{4}
We officially opened a company and even got our dream rooftop apartment
One apartment turned into two, then five.

When the rules became stricter in Barcelona, we adapted. {1}No tourist stays: we offer mid-term stays of 31+ nights, which is 100% legal without needing a license.{2} Literally anyone is allowed to rent out monthly stays in Barcelona (even on Airbnb), but not many people know this.

We don’t own any property. {1}We work with local owners.{2} We make a profit by renting big apartments with many bedrooms that are hard for them to rent out, and subletting the rooms individually with the owner’s permission.

We know how hard it can be to move alone to a new city, because we’ve been there ourselves. In Barcelona, scams are a real issue, and we’ve been through them: fake listings, lost deposits, endless paperwork, and dirty shared apartments with zero organization.
That’s why our mission is to offer a ready-to-move-in home to students, digital nomads and anyone living abroad, so they can simply arrive and start enjoying the city.
Then came the big one: our dream villa in Bali
We put all our savings into a very basic villa in Bali. {1}Scary AF.{2} We renovated it, made it beautiful and turned it into a mini luxury boutique hotel with three bedrooms.

We also officially opened a company in Bali and built a team here too. And the wildest part? {1}We now have rental properties in different parts of the world, and we still don’t own a single one of them.{2}
We didn’t just build an income stream. We built freedom.
Fast forward almost 10 years: {1}we run a profitable business with multiple properties around the world and a consistent passive income. And we started literally from zero.{2}

We believe that if you put love into your business, it comes right back to you. So we overpay our staff, work with the local communities, and set up our properties to give our guests an amazing 5-star experience. {1}It’s a win-win.{2}
When we started, we had no idea what we were doing. We learned everything the hard way, by trial and error and a lot of late nights.

{1}This course is everything we wish someone had told us back then.{2} It’s step by step and built from {3}real-life experience, not just theory.{4} Our course is designed to be your shortcut to business success.

Whether you want some extra income, homes in different places around the world, or a business that gives you more freedom, we’ll show you how, {1}so you can build your own property rental business without making the same mistakes we did.{2}
Will it always be easy? No. Is it possible? 100%.

If you’ve ever wanted to start your own business but thought you’d need a fortune to begin, this might be exactly what you’ve been looking for. {1}Most people assume a hosting business means buying property, taking out a mortgage or saving for years. It doesn’t.{2}
In reality, some of the most profitable hosts don’t own a single property, and neither do we.
There are different ways to make money as a host.

There are three main business models: {1}rental arbitrage, co-hosting and ownership.{2} With rental arbitrage and co-hosting, you can launch your hosting business without buying property. You don’t need a mortgage or a big down payment. What you do need is strategy and the right systems.
How much you need to start depends on the model. {1}With co-hosting, you can start with almost no money,{2} because you manage someone else’s property.
{1}With rental arbitrage, you do need some budget.{2} Before your first guest arrives, you pay the deposit, the first month’s rent and the furniture to make the place guest-ready.

{1}To give you an idea: for our apartments in Barcelona, we needed roughly €10,000 to get started.{2} Your number depends on the property and the location. It’s still a fraction of what buying would cost, and once you’re booked, you earn it back fast.

Already {1}own a property{2}? Even better. You’re sitting on an asset that can earn you money. By renting it out on a platform like Airbnb or Booking.com, you can earn much more from it, whether it’s a second home, an investment property or even just a spare room.
With the right setup, it can become a steady source of passive income.

Cities like Barcelona, Paris, New York City, and Amsterdam often require licenses, limit the number of rental nights, or restrict short-term rentals to certain zones.

{1}That doesn't mean strictly regulated places are a no-go.{2} We currently run multiple successful apartments in Barcelona, one of the most difficult cities for Airbnb. They don’t have a tourist license, but they’re all still legal.

{1}In Barcelona, anyone is allowed to create a listing on a platform like Airbnb without a license, as long as you host stays of 31 nights or more.{2} Not many people know this, and that’s exactly the opportunity.

While monthly stays tend to generate less income per night than short-term bookings, they’re still highly profitable. Plus, they come with fewer guest turnovers, less day-to-day management, and more stability. You might not even need a manager or a full-time team.

On the other hand, {1}some areas are much more flexible and easier to start in.{2} Places like Bali, parts of Mexico, Portugal, and Southern Spain are known for being more open to short-term rentals, especially in tourist-friendly zones or when offering longer stays. This is why choosing the right location is key.

Legal setup: private, self-employed or company?

Let’s be real, no one gets excited about legal paperwork. Luckily, you don’t need a complicated legal setup to get started. But it’s important to know your options and to declare your income from day one.

You have three main options: {1}rent out as a private individual, start as self-employed, or register a company.{2} Which one fits depends on your country, what you offer your guests and how big you want to grow.
Option 1: rent out as a private individual

Many people don’t know this: {1}in many countries you can rent out a place as a private person, without registering as self-employed or opening a company.{2} You simply declare the rental income on your personal tax return once a year, and you can usually deduct costs like rent, utilities, furniture and cleaning.
{1}You only rent out the space.{2} Cleaning between guests, keys and basic maintenance are normal for any landlord.
{1}You don’t offer hotel-like services during the stay,{2} such as a reception, daily cleaning, meals, laundry or airport transfers.
{1}You keep it small:{2} one or a few listings, and no staff on your payroll.

Once you start offering hotel-like services or grow into a real operation with staff, tax authorities usually see it as a business. Then you need to register as self-employed or open a company, and in some countries you also charge VAT.

If you rent out an apartment you own without hotel-like services, you declare it as rental income in your yearly income tax return (IRPF). No need to become autónomo. If you sublet a place you rent (rental arbitrage), the income is also taxed in your yearly return, unless it’s run as a business. Offer hotel-like services and it becomes a business: you register as autónomo and usually charge 10% VAT.

If you rent out one or a few places without extra services, you can do it as a private individual. You declare it on your yearly tax return: for the property, tax is based on its cadastral income ({1}kadastraal inkomen{2}), and if it’s furnished, 40% of the rent counts as income from the furniture. Offer services like breakfast or cleaning during the stay, and do it regularly? Then it becomes a professional activity: you register as self-employed (this can be a side activity, {3}zelfstandige in bijberoep{4}) and usually charge 6% VAT.

Most hosts report their rental income as rental income on Schedule E, without self-employment tax. If you provide substantial services, like daily cleaning, meals or concierge, it counts as a business (Schedule C).

{1}Always declare your income.{2} Since 2023, platforms like Airbnb and Booking.com share hosts’ income with the tax authorities for every listing in the EU. Renting out as a private individual doesn’t mean tax-free: it just means less admin.

Mindset, extra income and the tools you need.

Getting started is often the hardest part. It’s completely normal to feel uncertain, nervous, or even overwhelmed when stepping into something new. You might be thinking, “What if something goes wrong?” or “Am I really ready for this?” These doubts are common, but they’re also what keep most people stuck on the sidelines.

The truth is, {1}no one feels fully ready in the beginning. {2}Every successful host once stood exactly where you are now: unsure, questioning themselves, and wondering if they could actually do it. {3}What made the difference is that they took action anyway.{4}

Many people also feel resistance to {1}pitching landlords{2}, afraid they’ll say no. But many owners want exactly what you offer: rent paid on time and a well-kept property. {3}You only need one yes,{4} and Lesson 6 gives you the scripts.

If you want to succeed, you need to {1}shift your mindset from being just a host to thinking like a business owner. {2}Becoming a 6-figure host isn’t just about giving someone a nice place to sleep. {3}If you want to make real money, it’s about creating systems,{4} solving problems, managing relationships, and building something that can grow. A business owner makes decisions based on vision and long-term goals, not just today’s to-do list.

{1}You don’t need to have it all figured out. You just need to start. {2}Follow the steps in this course, one task at a time. You’ll learn by doing, gain confidence as you go, and build momentum with every small win.

Yes, you’ll face challenges. And yes, mistakes will happen. But every problem has a solution, and every obstacle is an opportunity to get better. Confidence doesn’t come from waiting until you’re ready. It comes from showing up anyway.

Thinking like a business owner also means looking at a property for what it {1}could{2} be, not for what it is today. Here are two of our apartments in Barcelona that taught us this the most.

Creative ways to make extra money (optional)
Being a host isn’t just about charging for a night’s stay. You can boost your income by offering extra services and experiences, many of which run on their own. Here are some creative ideas:

{1}Local partners and referral commissions:{2} Work with local businesses and earn a commission every time you send them a guest. Think of tour operators, surf lessons, motorbike rentals, restaurants, and websites with referral (affiliate) programs for event tickets and activities. The key is to think about what fits naturally with your property and your lifestyle. These add-ons can increase your income, improve guest satisfaction, and build a more memorable hosting brand with very little extra effort.

Most people think location is everything. And yes, being in a prime spot helps, but it's not the full story. {1}A great location with low demand will struggle. A less obvious location with high demand and the right setup? That can become a goldmine.{2}
Location matters, but demand is what drives bookings.
{1}Location is fixed.{2} It’s where your property is.
{1}Demand is dynamic.{2} It’s what people are searching for, when, and why.
Demand comes from two places. Sometimes people want to be in a certain area. And sometimes they want a certain property, wherever it is.

This is the classic case. Guests come for the city, the beach, a university, a hospital or an event, and they look for a place to sleep nearby. Here you compete with every other listing around you, so what counts is who comes, why, and when.
A beach town 20 minutes from a popular city might outperform a central apartment if it taps into weekend getaways and local tourism trends.
A quiet suburb near a hospital, university, or big event venue can have consistent bookings if you target the right audience (traveling nurses, researchers, digital nomads, etc.)

This is the part most new hosts miss. {1}Many guests don’t travel for the city at all. They travel for the stay.{2} They are not looking for a bed close to the supermarket or the metro. They are looking for an experience, and they are happy to drive an extra hour to get it.

When the property is the reason for the trip, a location that looks “bad” on paper stops being a problem. It can even become the selling point: quiet, private, surrounded by nature, far from everything.
A cabin or treehouse in the woods, an hour from the nearest city, that couples book for a weekend with no phone signal.
A villa in the middle of rice fields, 20 minutes from the beach and the restaurants, that guests choose for the view, the private pool and the silence.
A design house in a small village with nothing around it, booked for birthdays and anniversaries because of how it looks in the photos.
A farm stay or countryside house with a hot tub, a fireplace and animals, where families come to switch off for a few days.

In all of these, nobody searched for the village. They found a place they wanted to stay in, and then planned the trip around it. This also means less competition: you are not one of 300 similar apartments in the same neighborhood, you are the only place like yours.
So which one do you have?
{1}Don’t just chase the obvious tourist hotspots. {2}For every property you look at, ask:
Who is coming here, and why?
Are they coming for the area, or would they come for this property?
What kind of stays are most common: short trips, weekend getaways, monthly relocations?
If the location is average, what could make the stay special: a view, a pool, a hot tub, the design, total privacy?

The goal isn’t just to be in a “good area.” The goal is to have the right property for the right guest: either in a place people already want to be, or special enough that people come for it.

How to find the right property

Good news: you don’t need special “Airbnb-friendly” listings to get started. {1}For rental arbitrage, you can simply look at normal rental listings on normal property websites{2} and pitch your idea to the owner. You rent the place the normal way, but you come with a better offer. How to pitch it, you’ll learn in the next lesson.
Keep in mind that {1}for many homeowners, this will be the first time they hear about something like this.{2} That’s completely normal. Your job is to explain it clearly and make them feel safe.

Before you start looking, make sure you know the rules in your area (see {1}Lesson 2{2}). Check what’s allowed for short-term and mid-term stays, and whether you need a license. Some cities only allow short stays with a license, while mid-term stays of 31+ nights are fine (like in Barcelona). Subletting always needs the owner’s written permission in the contract.

Red flags to avoid when choosing a property

Not all properties are good for renting out to guests, whether you host short-term or mid-term stays, even if they look beautiful, cheap, or perfectly located. Some places come with hidden issues that can cost you time, money, and a ton of stress. The key is learning to spot these red flags before you commit.
Here’s what to watch out for:

If you’re looking at an apartment in a building with a homeowner’s association (HOA), make sure to ask about their rules for short-term rentals and subletting. Some buildings ban or heavily restrict short stays, while mid-term stays of a month or more are often fine. With short stays, a concierge or nosy neighbors will notice guest traffic quickly.
{1}Red flag:{2} Contracts that mention “no subletting,” “no commercial use,” or restrictions on guest frequency.

If a landlord seems uncomfortable with your plan or won’t give you permission in writing, don’t move forward. Vague verbal approvals won’t protect you if things go wrong. You want a clear agreement up front.
{1}Red flag:{2} Landlords who avoid the topic, say “let’s just see how it goes,” or refuse to put anything in writing.

Angry neighbors are one of the fastest ways to lose a listing. If you’re sharing walls with people who hate noise, guests, or strangers in the building, you’re asking for complaints and potential legal issues.
{1}Red flag:{2} Past conflicts in the building, complaints from other tenants, or extra-thin walls.

Guests value privacy, functionality, and comfort. Avoid properties with awkward layouts, no doors between sleeping areas, or bathrooms that feel exposed. This can lead to bad reviews and poor occupancy rates. Mid-term guests, like digital nomads, also need a good place to work and fast Wi-Fi.
{1}Red flag:{2} Studios trying to act like 2-bedrooms, shared bathrooms, or no soundproofing.

Location isn’t just about being central. It’s about being convenient. If the property is hard to find, far from transport, or has zero parking, it could turn off potential guests. Mid-term guests, like students and remote workers, also want shops, cafés and public transport nearby.
{1}Red flag:{2} Remote areas with no public transport or city apartments with expensive or no parking options.
Too much personal stuff or damage
Properties that are still full of the owner's belongings, expensive artwork, or delicate furniture can be a headache. Hosting requires a space that’s guest-ready, durable, and easy to clean.
{1}Red flag:{2} Cluttered units, sentimental or fragile items, and spaces that aren’t fully “handed over.”
If the unit has never been rented before and the landlord is unsure, treat it as a test. Try a shorter lease, or ask for a trial period to minimize your risk.
{1}Red flag:{2} High rent, no data to support demand, or landlords who expect full-year commitment without flexibility.

{1}Bottom line:{2} It’s better to walk away from a risky deal than to regret it later. Trust your gut, do your research, and don’t compromise on legal clarity, location quality, or guest experience. A solid property sets the foundation for a stress-free, profitable hosting business.

Why? Because you're solving a real problem for them.

Most landlords want exactly three things: reliable income, a well-maintained property, and as little stress as possible. Traditional long-term tenants can bring risks like late payments, poor communication, damage, or even legal disputes.
With rental arbitrage, you offer a smart alternative:

When you're pitching to a landlord, keep this in mind: if they’re renting out a property, they likely own at least two (one to live in and one to rent). That often means they’re business-minded or entrepreneurial.
They may be more open than you think, especially when they see that you treat this like a serious business, not a casual side hustle.

Your success as a host depends on keeping their place in top condition because bad reviews kill bookings. That means it's in your best interest to take better care of their property than most long-term tenants ever would.

To build trust, show your systems. Walk them through the cleaning checklist, guest communication templates, and SOPs (you’ll find them all in this course). Show them you’re not just winging it, you’re running a well-organized, guest-focused business. And that gives them peace of mind.

Most importantly, make it clear that you deeply respect the neighbors and community. You screen guests, respect the house rules, and maintain quiet hours because happy neighbors mean long-term success. Position your offer right, and you’re not just asking for permission. You’re offering a win-win.

Before you pitch: two case studies

What you pitch matters as much as how you pitch it. If you email every one- and two-bedroom flat on the market, you’ll hear “no” over and over, because those are exactly the places a landlord can rent to anyone. {1}The fastest yes comes from the property the landlord struggles to rent.{2} Here are two real cases from our own business, in two very different markets, so you know what to look for before you send a single email.
{1}Case study · Europe{2}Barcelona: big apartments, rented room by room
In Barcelona, what works best for us are {1}big apartments with 4 to 6 bedrooms{2}. The historic centre is full of them, and owners find them hard to rent out:
The rent is often too high for a couple.

{1}The people who are interested are often the wrong tenants.{2} Usually it’s a group of young people. Many of them would sublet the rooms anyway, illegally, and some throw parties. That’s exactly what the owner is afraid of.
{1}Families rarely live there.{2} They usually don’t want to live in the busy, touristic centre.

That’s your opening. You do the same thing those tenants would do, but legally, professionally and with everything organised and under control. You rent the whole apartment, furnish it, give it a fresh coat of paint, and rent out the rooms one by one: as coliving or mid-term stays, or short-term where the law allows it. {1}The owner gets the entire apartment rented on one contract{2}, rent on time, and a home that is painted and maintained far more often than with a normal tenant.

In Bali, renting a property and subletting it legally is very common, so you don’t need much convincing, as long as your company and paperwork are in order. The number of bedrooms matters much less too: one to four bedrooms can all work, {1}as long as the rent makes sense for the return you can get.{2}
The catch: {1}you pay much more up front.{2} In Bali you don’t rent a place month to month.

Most properties are rented on a {1}leasehold{2}: you pay for a fixed number of years in one go, often 25. When the lease ends, the property goes back to the owner, together with everything you built or improved on it.

You can also find leases for fewer years. We first took Casa Mewali (our small boutique villa, where we also rent out the rooms individually) for {1}3 years{2}, with the right to extend written into the contract. Because you’re not paying the price of buying a property, it was still very affordable.

We chose Casa Mewali because its setup is perfect for our coliving model: a shared pool with individual bedrooms around it. Instead of trying to rent out the entire villa, we divide it up and rent out the bedrooms one by one.
Casa Mewali, our small boutique villa in Bali.

{1}Why rooms and not the whole villa?{2} Most hosts in Bali rent out the entire villa, so that’s where the competition is. But a lot of travellers, many of them girls who love taking beautiful pictures, dream of staying in a villa this pretty and can’t afford the whole place. A single bedroom they can afford. That’s why people love booking this one.

Downstairs, 2 bedrooms open onto the pool, each with its own bathroom. Upstairs there is a third bedroom, also with its own bathroom. So: 3 suites around the pool, with the kitchen separate at the entrance. You give them the same stable income, with more care for the property. The rent is guaranteed and on time, and if they ever want to go back to a traditional tenant, you handle the transition.
You screen every guest, enforce quiet hours and respectful behavior, and there’s always a local contact for emergencies and a direct line of communication.
“Why don’t you just rent it normally?”
Because this is a business, not a side hustle. Explain how your model gives the landlord stable rent, while you handle all the headaches of guest turnover, cleaning, and communication.

You can also show them what they gain compared with a classic long-term contract, where they are tied to the same tenant for years. With this model they keep flexibility: they don’t have to wait for a long contract to end to get their property back. If they have an emergency or simply need the property, they can ask for it back with a much shorter notice period. And on top of that, you take out rental insurance.
{1}Extra card to play{2}Offer to improve the apartment yourself

If you find an apartment with real potential, here is one more card you can play: {1}offer to make some improvements at your own cost.{2} For the same rent, the landlord gets a better apartment. That can be exactly what turns a “maybe” into a “yes”.

In one of our apartments, we replaced the old floor and turned the bathtub into a shower, which is also much easier for regular cleaning. The floor looked very old, and just changing it gave the whole apartment a makeover. Because the apartment looked so much better, we could rent the rooms at our prices and earn more.

You’re taking this apartment as an investment, so you already have a budget for setting it up. Include the cost of the improvements in that budget and in your {1}profit calculator{2}, and check that the higher prices you can ask pay it back.
{1}Ask first.{2} Maybe the landlord is willing to do or pay for the work. It’s a negotiation, so start there.
{1}Keep it as a card to play{2} when the landlord hesitates, not as your opening offer.
{1}Only if the numbers work.{2} The improvement has to pay for itself within your contract.

Take quality photos without hiring a pro

You don’t need to spend hundreds on a professional photographer to create a high-converting listing. With the right approach, you can take stunning photos yourself, even with a smartphone. The key is understanding what guests want to see and how to showcase your space in the best possible light.

Before taking any pictures, make sure everything is spotless and styled. Open the curtains, fluff the pillows, and hide cords, visible bins and remotes. The photos must show the place as it really is, but you can remove items that make it look cluttered. Think of it like setting the stage; you want it to look welcoming, calm, and inviting.

Natural light is your best friend. Shoot during the day when your space is the brightest, ideally in the morning or late afternoon. Turn off overhead lights to avoid yellow tones. Open windows and let daylight in.
3. Use a good phone or camera
Most modern smartphones are more than enough. Just make sure your lens is clean and the resolution is set to high quality. Avoid using filters or heavy editing. Guests want to see the real space.
Always take photos in landscape mode (horizontal), not vertical. Airbnb displays your listing photos in landscape, so this format gives a better view of each space.

Stand in corners or doorways to get as much of the room in the shot as possible. Use a wide-angle setting if available, but don’t distort the room. Guests want a real sense of space, not a fisheye view. On an iPhone Pro, the 0.5 lens works best.
Show everything: entryway, closets, appliances, amenities, parking, balcony, views. If it adds value, capture it. Lack of transparency leads to bad reviews.
7. Your photo order matters (this is crucial for bookings).

{1}Your first picture is your million-dollar shot.{2} It’s what sells your listing, and it matters more than anything else: it’s what brings in the clicks, the bookings and the income. Use your most eye-catching image as cover photo. Bedrooms usually perform best. Follow up with 4 key shots of different rooms that highlight your space’s best features. Airbnb shows only the first 5 photos before guests have to click “Show all photos,” so this is where you make a strong first impression and grab their attention.
Check out our listing as an example
The first five photos are all a guest sees before clicking

Sometimes the smallest details make the biggest difference. In one of our Barcelona apartments, we had two identical rooms; same size, same layout, just mirrored. Yet one was always fully booked, while the other struggled to get reservations unless we dropped the price.

Visually, the desk in the popular room made the space look bigger and more inviting. That slight design edge translated into significantly better performance and higher profit. We swapped out the less appealing desk, and suddenly both rooms booked out at full price.
The takeaway: If your bookings are slow, take a hard look at your listing. Tiny design choices can cost you money.
Instead of just showing rooms, capture little moments such as a cup on the coffee table, cozy blankets, books on a nightstand. It makes guests imagine themselves staying there.

Photos are the most important part of your listing. This is where you sell your space before guests read the description. A great listing with bad photos won’t get bookings. But even a simple space with beautiful, clear, well-lit images can perform incredibly well.
So if photography isn’t your strength, consider asking a friend with a good eye or hiring someone locally. It’s a small investment that can pay off big.
Important listing details that protect you
This section can save you from headaches, bad reviews, and refund requests.
Your listing description isn’t just a sales pitch. It’s also your legal shield. Whatever you clearly mention in writing can protect you from guest complaints, refund requests, and bad reviews.
So don’t hold back. Be honest, be detailed, and include everything that could potentially become a problem.
Here’s what to include: {1}House rules: {2} Be clear and specific. No smoking? Quiet hours? Visitors allowed? Extra fee for late check-in? Spell it all out. Don’t assume people will “just know.”
Is there potential for noise from nearby bars? Are there stairs, shared spaces, or pets on the property? Mention them all.

If your listing is not fully private, you need to state this clearly and more than once. Even if it’s already mentioned in the listing, repeat it in the description. Put it in CAPITALS. Make it obvious. Some guests will still “miss it” and claim they didn’t know. If it’s written clearly, Airbnb will side with you.

Include a statement like: "In case of disrespectful, aggressive, or intoxicated behavior, the host reserves the right to cancel the reservation without refund to protect the property and maintain a safe environment.”
It might feel like you’re being overly cautious, but trust us: you’re not. You’re protecting your peace and your business.
The more transparent you are, the fewer problems you’ll have. Take time to list everything that matters.

Guests accept your house rules before booking, so they protect you as a host. But Airbnb has new rules for this. For bookings made from 20 November 2026, your house rules must be in the house rules section of your listing before guests book. You can’t add new rules later by message, with signs in the home or in person.

Your rules must also be reasonable. That means {1}no fines or penalties, no extra fees{2} for things that are part of your listing, and {3}no chores a cleaner would normally do{4}, like washing dishes, stripping the bed or taking the trash out of the building. Small requests, like putting used dishes in the sink, are still fine. Keep your rules short and clear: guests actually read them that way.

to stay competitive from day one

Setting the right price is one of the most important factors for your success, especially when you're just getting started. If your price is too high, your listing won’t get traction. Too low, and you might fill your calendar but leave money on the table.
Here’s how to price smart from day one:

When your listing is new and doesn’t have reviews yet, guests are taking a small risk by booking. To overcome that, offer a competitive introductory price (10–20% below market average). This helps you get your first few bookings and collect 5-star reviews faster which boosts your search ranking.

Tools like PriceLabs, Wheelhouse, or Airbnb’s Smart Pricing adjust your nightly rate based on demand, seasonality, events, and competitor pricing. These tools help you avoid undercharging on busy weekends or high seasons.
Pro tip: Airbnb’s Smart Pricing tends to undervalue your listing. Use it with caution and always set a minimum price you’re comfortable with.
Research similar listings in your area. Look at:
If they’re booked out and you’re not, it’s likely a pricing (or photo) issue. Adjust accordingly.
To encourage longer stays and fill your calendar, set smart discounts for weekly and monthly bookings. This can help increase occupancy and reduce turnover work, especially during slower seasons.
5. Don’t rely on just the nightly rate
Your cleaning fee and minimum stay also impact how attractive your listing is. If your cleaning fee is too high compared to your nightly rate, it might drive guests away, especially for short stays.
Once you have at least 5 strong reviews and some social proof, you can gradually increase your prices. Don’t make a big jump overnight; test small increases and monitor your bookings.
Airbnb offers tools like “early bird” discounts, “last-minute” discounts, and promotions for new listings. Use them strategically to stay booked without cheapening your brand.
Pricing is never “set it and forget it.” Revisit your strategy every week or two, especially in the beginning. Stay flexible, use data, and optimize based on results, not just assumptions.
With the right pricing strategy, you can stay competitive, attract quality guests, and build up your income from the very first listing.

Setting clear expectations upfront is one of the most effective ways to avoid misunderstandings, prevent complaints, and ensure a smooth experience for both you and your guests.
Before a guest even books, your listing should clearly communicate exactly what they’re getting. This includes things like:
Whether the space is private or shared
Rules about visitors, smoking, or pets
Layout of the space and shared areas
Location details (e.g., if it’s in a lively area or a quiet neighborhood)
Any limitations or quirks (e.g., steep stairs, construction nearby, no elevator)
It might feel like you’re pointing out negatives, but transparency builds trust. It also protects you. If issues come up, you can always point back to what was clearly mentioned before booking.
Here’s where you should reinforce expectations:
Your listing description and house rules
The welcome message right after booking
Signage or reminders in the property (when necessary)
It’s okay to repeat the same things several times, especially if guests share common spaces.

Being honest doesn’t scare good guests away. It filters out the ones who aren’t the right fit, and those are often the ones who create problems. Setting expectations early makes your life easier, your reviews better, and your hosting stress-free.
How to make guests follow your rules: make them clear
{1}Write rules that are specific.{2} “Check-out is strictly at 11:00 AM” works. “Please be respectful” does not.
{1}Put them in your house rules.{2} Guests have to accept them before booking, so you can always refer back to them.
{1}Repeat them.{2} In the listing description, in the welcome message, and on signs or labels inside the property.
{1}Keep them short.{2} Guests are tired when traveling and ignore long texts.
{1}Be polite but firm when a rule is broken.{2} Point to the rule they agreed to.

We mention in our listing seven times that the kitchen and pool are shared, plus one final reminder in the welcome message. And still, occasionally, a guest arrives claiming we didn't mention it and asks for a full refund.

The reality is: some people simply don’t read. But that’s their responsibility, not yours. As long as you’ve clearly stated it in multiple places, you’re fully protected. If you can prove it was communicated upfront, guests will accept that they made a mistake, and Airbnb will side with you.

If something could affect the guest experience, like construction noise nearby, frame it as a benefit rather than a problem. For example, mention in your listing that the current rate already includes a special discount due to temporary construction in the area.

This way, guests feel like they’re getting a deal. Often, you don’t even need to reduce your price significantly. Just highlighting that a discount has been applied makes guests think, “I’m getting a great offer,” rather than focusing on the inconvenience. It's all about how you position it.
How to handle complaints or damages

We personally started by doing everything ourselves, not because we wanted to, but because we didn’t have the budget for a team in the beginning. And honestly, it was one of the best ways to learn the business inside out. But let’s be real: cleaning toilets and fixing light bulbs isn’t what grows your business.
While it’s helpful to understand how every part works, the manager role is by far the most important. That’s the person who keeps operations running, guests happy, and problems solved.

Our recommendation: start small but strategic. Begin by hiring one cleaner (and make sure you also have a backup option), and find a reliable freelance handyman who can handle basic maintenance. {1}You don’t have to hire them officially.{2} If you rent out as a private individual or as self-employed, you can work with them as freelancers. Just put your agreement in writing: that’s always better for both sides.
Then, for the first few weeks, manage the listing yourself. Respond to guests, handle check-ins, deal with minor issues, and file damage requests with Airbnb.
This will teach you the platform, the guest journey, and the kinds of things that actually come up.

Once that’s running smoothly and you know what the job involves, you’ll be in a much better position to hire a manager. You’ll understand how long tasks take, what tools they need, and what quality looks like.
Ideally, your manager should live near the property so they can also serve as the emergency contact, someone who can be on-site quickly if there’s ever an issue while you’re away.

You gradually remove yourself from daily tasks without losing oversight
Remember: you don’t need to work in your business. You want a business that works FOR you!

When to expand (and when to wait)
Deciding to expand is one of the most exciting milestones in your hosting journey. {1}But growing too fast or too soon can backfire.{2} Be honest with yourself and tick what’s true today:
{1}Your current listing runs like a well-oiled machine:{2} Systems are in place, guests are happy, reviews are great, and operations don’t depend on you 24/7.
{1}You’ve built a reliable team:{2} Cleaners, a handyman, and a manager or co-host are already trained and capable of handling turnovers and guest issues without your direct involvement.
{1}You’ve automated repetitive tasks:{2} Messaging, pricing, and check-ins run with minimal input thanks to tools like automated messaging, dynamic pricing tools, and smart locks.
{1}You consistently turn a profit:{2} Your current property is generating reliable income, even during low season.
{1}You have capital (or cash flow) to invest:{2} Expansion requires upfront costs. If you don’t have a buffer, the stress can outweigh the rewards.
{1}You’re still figuring out your systems:{2} If your current property requires constant attention or if things often go wrong, focus on refining your process first.
{1}Your reviews are mixed or inconsistent:{2} Expanding while you're still trying to deliver a great guest experience can compound problems and hurt your reputation.
{1}You don’t have a strong team in place:{2} Trying to manage two properties without support will lead to burnout and mistakes.
{1}Cash flow is tight:{2} Stretching your budget can put pressure on the guest experience, maintenance, and quality, which hurts long-term success.
Expanding too soon is one of the most common mistakes new hosts make. A second listing should feel like a natural next step, not a leap of faith.

Over time, shared spaces like the kitchen and bathroom can get cluttered with items left behind by previous guests or tenants, especially in longer stays or co-living setups. This creates mess, confusion, and even hygiene issues.

To maintain a clean, welcoming space for everyone, it’s important to periodically reset and declutter. Here’s a simple system you can use to clear shared areas without causing misunderstandings or tension.
There are two main approaches that we recommend to avoid removing items that are still in use.
Designate a specific spot for unclaimed or leftover items, like a basket in the bathroom or a drawer in the freezer. Let guests know that anything placed there will be removed after a set deadline.
This method works especially well for things like shampoo bottles, freezer items, or personal belongings left in shared spaces.
Place a roll of tape and a marker near shared storage areas (like the fridge door or pantry). Ask guests to label their items with their name. Anything left unlabeled will be cleared out.
Shampoo and soap bottles in the shower

Start with a full cleaning of shared areas, especially the kitchen, bathroom, and hallway. This is the best time to spot forgotten items, expired food, or things taking up unnecessary space. Depending on the decluttering method you choose, either place these items in a designated removal spot or start labeling them with tape and a marker.

Even if you've spoken to someone in person, follow up with a message to set clear expectations and avoid any surprises. Include a short deadline and explain the decluttering method to identify or collect their items. Make sure to send a reminder the day before you are removing the items.
